feedback: If a wind direction seems reversed, return to this map’s key. Meteorological wind is named by where it comes from; a motion arrow may point where it goes, while a conventional wind-barb staff extends toward the direction it comes from.
If a learner assumes a symbol is self-evident, point back to the key and ask them to decode fronts, wind barbs or pressure explicitly.
Read wind speed only from the encodings this map specifies, such as barb feathers, a numeric label, arrow length or colour. Do not infer a speed when the key gives no speed encoding.
If a learner says the map shows the weather everywhere all the time, clarify it is a snapshot or forecast for a particular moment or period.
activities.intendedInsight: A weather map is a decodable instrument, not decoration: many symbols (fronts, wind barbs, pressure) must be read from a key rather than guessed, and a map is a snapshot/forecast for a moment or period, not the weather everywhere all the time.
learnerActions: Study a labelled weather map showing temperature figures, weather icons (e.g. sun, cloud, rain), wind symbols (arrows or barbs), and front/pressure symbols.

Use the actual map’s key to decode temperature, precipitation, fronts, pressure and wind. State wind direction and speed only as encoded by that key, including any arrow length, colour, label or barb markings.

Name wind by the direction it comes from. Check the map’s key to decide whether a wind arrow points toward its destination or a staff extends toward its origin, and translate that symbol into the correct from-direction.
Explain, for a named front or pressure symbol, what weather it tends to bring.
activities.title: Crack the code: decode a real weather map

feedback: If a learner misreads the graph axis or reads between gridlines wrongly, have them track from the point to the labelled axis and re-check the units; a value off the scale or the wrong day signals this error.
If a learner treats one day's value as the whole pattern, prompt: look across all the points before naming a pattern.
If a learner assumes a high number means bad weather, ask what is being measured and in what units.
activities.intendedInsight: A trend requires a series of readings — a single data point is not a pattern — and correct reading depends on checking the axis scale and units, since higher numbers do not automatically mean 'worse' weather.
learnerActions: Read a time-series table or graph of weather data (e.g. temperature or rainfall over a week, month or season).
Extract specific values when asked: the highest temperature, which day was wettest, the value on a named day.
Track a finger from each data point to the labelled axis and check the units before reporting a value.
Look across ALL the data points and name the trend (e.g. temperatures rising through the week, rainfall decreasing, pressure falling).
activities.title: Read the data and name the trend

feedback: For a wrong symbol answer, return to the key (and, for wind, check that map's own direction convention and whether the direction or the speed encoding was misread).
For a graph-reading error, re-track from point to axis and re-check units.
For an ungrounded prediction, ask which trend in the data supports it.
activities.intendedInsight: Symbol meaning, pattern identification, and data-based prediction can each be checked directly, surfacing whether the learner can apply the interpretation procedure.
learnerActions: Answer targeted questions: 'What does this symbol mean?', 'What pattern does this graph show?', and 'Predict from this data.'
Select or state the correct value read from a specific graph or table.
Choose or state a prediction that follows from the shown trend and justify the choice.
activities.title: Symbol- and graph-reading checks (companion assessment)
